body.p: Preparing HTML Files for Accurate DITA-XML Conversion

concept.abstract: This section describes the purpose and audience of this guide as well as the prerequisites for HTML conversion to DITA-XML. It covers the mandatory and optional HTML constructs, document preparation requirements, and the scenarios that affect conversion readiness. The converter and AI Agent use these structures to detect document hierarchy, classify topic types, infer metadata, and generate accurate DITA maps and topic files.

concept.shortdesc: This guide provides mandatory best practices for anyone who creates or prepares HTML source content

conbody.p: This guide provides mandatory best practices for anyone who creates or prepares HTML source content for conversion to DITA-XML using the metR DocMigration HTML to DITA converter. The converter is a modular microservice with an embedded AI Agent that reasons and enriches DITA elements in document structure before transforming them into standards-compliant DITA-XML.
Following these guidelines ensures that:

ul.li: The converter correctly identifies topic boundaries, heading hierarchies, and content types.
The AI Conversion Agent classifies topics accurately as concept, task, reference, or troubleshooting.
The generated DITA-XML output is clean and complete, requiring minimal post-conversion cleanup.
Metadata and Ditamap hierarchies are detected reliably.

conbody.p: This guide is intended for the following audiences:

Reference when reviewing or auditing source documents before migration projects.

conbody.note: You must have basic working knowledge of HTML heading levels, links, tables, lists, images, and metadata. This guide assumes that you can inspect HTML in a browser and, when needed, in source view.

section.p: The metR HTML to DITA converter does not rely on visual formatting alone. It reads structural information from HTML elements and semantic markup. When those elements are applied correctly, the converter and AI Agent can:

ul.li: Generate a root Ditamap and child Ditamaps from the index file, ZIP folder name, or document title.
Detect topic boundaries from heading levels and establish the Ditamap hierarchy.
Classify topic types: concept (descriptive), task (procedural), reference (tabular or lookup), or troubleshooting.
Convert paragraphs, lists, tables, images, links, inline formatting, and code blocks to valid DITA elements.
Infer metadata — short descriptions, keywords, index terms, author, and revision history — from <head> meta tags and structured body elements.
Flag issues such as missing short descriptions, invalid links, duplicate IDs, orphan topics, and improper nesting for human review.

concept.abstract: This section describes the typical structure of an HTML package submitted for conversion to DITA-XML, including folder organization, file naming, and the placement of media assets. It covers the standard HTML page structure the converter expects, focusing on how both <head> metadata and <body> content is read and mapped. The converter uses these structures to identify the entry point, build the root and child Ditamap hierarchy, determine topic boundaries from heading levels, and generate accurate DITA maps and topic files.

concept.shortdesc: A typical HTML package contains the following:

conbody.p: A typical HTML package contains the following:
conbody.codeblock: HTML Package (ZIP) ├── index.html → creates the root Ditamap hierarchy (if present) ├── topic1.html → creates a child Ditamap and DITA topic ├-- topic2.html → creates a child Ditamap and DITA topic ├── media/ │ ├── image1.png │ └── image2.svg ├── css/ │ └── styles.css → ignored └── scripts/ └── script.js → ignored
conbody.p: The converter reads the HTML constructs given in the following bullet list:

ul.li: Index file ( index.html , optional). Creates the root Ditamap hierarchy and serves as the entry point for the converted documentation.
HTML files ( .html or .htm ). The converter creates a child Ditamap and a primary DITA topic from each file.
Images and media. The converter maps referenced assets to DITA <image> elements.

conbody.p: The converter reads the package structure to create the root Ditamap folder hierarchy, identifies the main entry point, preserves relative paths for images and media, and generates child Ditamaps based on individual HTML files. Submit HTML content as a ZIP file.
conbody.note: Organize HTML files in a logical folder structure before conversion. The converter preserves the folder hierarchy in the DITA output.

concept.shortdesc: Each HTML file follows standard HTML5 document structure:

conbody.p: Each HTML file follows standard HTML5 document structure:
conbody.codeblock: <html> <head> <title>Page Title</title> <meta name="author" content="Documentation Team"> <meta name="created" content="2026-01-15"> </head> <body> [Content appears here] <footer> [Footer content] </footer> </body> </html>
conbody.p: The converter focuses on two key areas:

ol.li: <head> metadata. The converter maps this content to DITA <prolog> elements such as author, created date, and revised date
<body> content. The converter maps this content to DITA topic body elements, including paragraphs, lists, tables, and images.

conbody.note: The converter ignores footer content by default, as well as CSS, JavaScript, navigation menus, cookie banners, advertisements, and hidden elements. If your HTML file contains important content in the footer, move it to the <body> section before conversion.

conbody.p: The <body> element contains semantic content that maps to DITA topics and topic body elements. The converter processes elements in document order and uses the heading hierarchy to determine topic boundaries and nesting levels.
The converter extracts the HTML package, analyzes metadata and content structure, applies heading-based hierarchy rules, and generates the corresponding Ditamaps and topics.
conbody.note: If the HTML uses visual formatting instead of semantic structure, the converter may append content to the wrong topic, create an incorrect hierarchy, or generate DITA that requires manual cleanup.

concept.abstract: This section covers the Table of Contents and Root Index — the navigation structure that maps the publication hierarchy and serves as the converter's primary entry point for building the root DITA map — and two scenarios: a root index file present in the package, and a missing root index file. The converter reads the root index to construct the DITA map hierarchy and topic references; when no root index is present, it falls back to the package folder name or filename as the root map title.

conbody.p: A table of contents or root index is the navigation structure of a publication. It declares the document's complete hierarchy in one place — the titles, sequence, and parent-child relationships of all sections, chapters, and topics — and provides the entry point from which readers and systems navigate the entire deliverable.

For the publishing system, the table of contents or root index is the structural anchor of the entire output — every generated navigation artifact, including the PDF bookmark panel, the HTML5 navigation tree, the WebHelp TOC panel, and the DITA map hierarchy, derives from this structure.
conbody.note: The converter reads it to build the DITA map hierarchy and then discards it — the publishing transform regenerates the navigation structure at build time from the assembled DITA map, ensuring it always reflects the actual content rather than a manually maintained list that can fall out of sync.
conbody.p: In a well-structured HTML package, the table of contents is provided by the navigation structure in the index.html or index.htm file. Each navigation link references an HTML document within the publication, and the order and nesting of these links establish the hierarchy of the generated documentation.

The converter reads the navigation structure in the index file to generate the root Ditamap hierarchy. The table of contents itself is not converted into a standalone DITA topic. Instead, each navigation link becomes a corresponding <mapref> or <topicref> in the generated root Ditamap, preserving the organization of the original HTML publication.
conbody.note: Ensure that the table of contents accurately reflects the intended publication hierarchy and that every navigation link references a valid HTML file. Missing, incorrect, or incomplete navigation links result in an incomplete Ditamap hierarchy and may exclude topics from the generated publication.

concept.abstract: This section covers meta tags and structured metadata elements in HTML — the metadata fields that identify, attribute, and classify a document independently of its body content — and one scenario: <head> meta tags populated in the source file and mapped during conversion. The converter reads each recognized meta tag and maps it to the corresponding DITA <prolog> element, making the document's authorship, dates, and classification data available to downstream publishing and search tools.

conbody.p: Metadata is structured information about a document, separate from its body content. It records attributes such as authorship, creation and revision dates, and classification tags. This information is what allows downstream publishing systems, content management platforms, and search indexes to reliably identify, track, and retrieve the document.

In HTML documents, metadata lives in two places: the <head> section as <meta> tags, and occasionally in the document <body> as CMS-generated structured elements such as Confluence's <div class="page-metadata"> block. Both carry the same categories of information but in different forms that the converter must recognize and extract from each location.
The converter and AI Agent map this metadata to the DITA <prolog> element in the generated topic, making it available to downstream publishing tools, content management systems, and search indexes.

<meta name="last-modified"> or text parsed from last modified on...

conbody.note: Metadata not found in the HTML source, or in an unrecognized format, is not included in the DITA output. Add it manually after conversion or ensure the source uses a supported format before submitting.

reference.shortdesc: Scenario 1 — HTML metadata mapped to <prolog> Consider an HTML document where the author

section.p: Consider an HTML document where the author has provided metadata using standard <meta> tags inside the <head> section, covering author, creation and revision dates, keywords, and a short description.

entry.codeblock: <head> <title>Configuring Network Settings</title> <meta name="author" content="XYZ"/> <meta name="created" content="2025-03-14"/> <meta name="last-modified" content="2025-11-02"/> <meta name="keywords" content="network, configuration, setup"/> <meta name="description" content="Steps to configure the device network settings."/> <meta name="company" content="XYZ Corp"/> </head>

<concept id="configuring_network_settings"> <title>Configuring Network Settings</title> <prolog> <author>XYZ</author> <critdates> <created date="2025-03-14"/> <revised modified="2025-11-02"/> </critdates> <metadata> <keywords> <keyword>network</keyword> <keyword>configuration</keyword> <keyword>setup</keyword> </keywords> <othermeta name="company" content="XYZ Corp"/> </metadata> </prolog> <shortdesc>Steps to configure the device network settings.</shortdesc> <conbody> ... </conbody> </concept>

section.p: Result: Each recognized <meta> tag is mapped to its corresponding DITA <prolog> element — author maps to <author>, created and last-modified map to <critdates><created> and <critdates><revised>, and keywords maps to a list of <keyword> elements inside <metadata>. The description meta tag maps to <shortdesc>, and company maps to <othermeta name="company"> since it has no dedicated DITA prolog element. The <title> element supplies the topic title.

concept.abstract: This section covers the Heading style in HTML — its role as the primary structural mechanism that organizes a document's content into a named, hierarchical sequence of sections — and four scenarios: headings applied in correct sequential order, a heading level skipped in the hierarchy, a top-level heading absent from the document, and consecutive headings with no body content between them. The converter reads each heading level to construct the DITA map hierarchy, generating sub-maps, topic files, and topic type classifications from the heading sequence and the content that follows each heading.

conbody.p: A Headingstyle marks the beginning of a named section of content and assigns it a rank in the document hierarchy. It is the primary structural mechanism of any technical document — headings divide continuous content into discrete, named units, establish the parent-child relationships between those units, and create the navigational backbone that readers and publishing systems depend on.

The heading hierarchy is expressed through levels: a top-level heading (Heading 1) names a major section; each lower-level heading (Heading 2 through Heading N) names a subsection within its parent. This ranked sequence carries the same structural meaning regardless of the format it is expressed. The level communicates the section's position in the hierarchy; the text communicates its subject.
conbody.note: Only a semantically marked heading — applied through the document's native heading mechanism — creates a genuine section boundary that a converter, search engine, or publishing system can detect and act on.
conbody.p: In well-formed HTML, headings are applied sequentially without skipping levels. An <h1> is followed by one or more <h2> elements, each <h2> may contain one or more <h3> elements, and so on.

The converter reads the heading elements within the <body> of each HTML file to determine how many DITA topic files to generate, how to title and nest them in the Ditamap, and what topic type each one receives. It then analyzes the content that follows each heading, such as paragraphs, lists, and tables, to classify the resulting topic as Concept, Task, Reference, Troubleshooting, or Generic.
The following table shows how each HTML heading element maps to a DITA construct:

concept.abstract: This section covers Lists in HTML — the primary structure for presenting discrete, parallel items in a defined or co-equal sequence — and introduces two subsections: Ordered Lists and Unordered Lists. The converter reads the list type, nesting level, and topic context to determine whether to map each list to <ol>, <ul>, <steps>, <substeps>, <choices>, or <dl> in the DITA output.

conbody.p: Listscommunicate sequences, collections, and term-definition pairs that prose paragraphs cannot organize with equal clarity. They are the primary structure for presenting discrete, parallel items — steps in a procedure, items in a requirements checklist, and options in a configuration section.
A list communicates to the reader that its items share a structural relationship: either sequence matters and the order is meaningful, or the items are co-equal and interchangeable in position.

The converter evaluates the HTML list type together with its surrounding context — topic classification, position relative to other content, and nesting — to generate the appropriate DITA list structure. Ordered lists, unordered lists, and term lists are each governed by their own mapping rules, described in the sections that follow.
conbody.note: Always use native HTML list elements (ol and ul) to represent structured information. Do not simulate lists using manually typed numbers, bullet characters, hyphens, or spacing within paragraphs, as these patterns are treated as plain text during conversion.

concept.abstract: This section covers Ordered Lists in HTML — items presented in a defined sequence where position is significant — and twenty-one scenarios grouped across six categories: consecutive and discontinuous numbered lists as procedures and workflows, single-item numbered lists, two-level and three-level nested numbered lists, and interrupted numbered lists where an admonition, paragraph, image, table, or bullet list appears between items. The converter maps each ordered list to <ol><li> in concept and reference topics, or to <steps><step><cmd> in task topics, based on the heading classification and content context.

conbody.p: An ordered list presents items in a defined sequence where the position of each item is significant. The ordered lists are universally used for step-by-step procedures, installation instructions, and ranked items.

For the reader, a numbered list communicates that sequence is contractual — item 2 depends on item 1 being completed, and performing the items out of order produces an incorrect or unsafe result. It is also a navigational reference that lets a reader say "I am on step 4" and return to the correct position after an interruption.

The list level is controlled by the Increase and Decrease Indent buttons, determines nesting depth: level 1 is the top level, level 2 is the first nested level, level 3 is the second, and so on. Sometimes they are also defined by their tab indentation. The list level assigned by list controls is what drives the nesting structure in the DITA output.

In well-structured HTML, ordered lists are created using native <ol> and <li> elements. Nested ordered lists represent subordinate sequences, while introductory paragraphs, images, tables, and notes provide supporting information without changing the sequential relationship between list items. A new <ol> element beginning after an existing list — rather than continuing it — signals a restarted or independent sequence rather than a continuation of the prior list.

The converter evaluates both the HTML list structure and the classified DITA topic type when processing an ordered list. Within Concept, Reference, and Generic topics, an HTML <ol> is converted to a DITA <ol>. Within a Task topic, the same <ol> is converted into <steps>, with each <li> mapped to a <step> containing a <cmd>. The surrounding context determines how supporting content associated with each list item is represented in the generated DITA structure.

concept.abstract: This section covers Term Lists (Definition Lists) in HTML — structures that associate a term with its corresponding definition or description, emphasizing term-description relationships rather than value comparison across columns — and two scenarios: a native HTML <dl> element with <dt> and <dd> pairs, and a <ul> list following the bold-label pattern where each <li> begins with a <strong> term followed by a separator and definition text. The converter maps each term list to <dl><dlentry><dt><dd> in concept and reference topics, or nests it inside <step><info> as supporting information in task topics, based on the heading classification and content context.

conbody.p: A term list, also known as a definition list, is an HTML structure used to associate terms with their corresponding definitions or descriptions. It is commonly used to present technical terminology, configuration options, error codes, connection modes, and other reference information, with each term followed by one or more explanatory statements. Unlike a table, a definition list emphasizes the relationship between a term and its description rather than comparing values across multiple columns.

Term lists improve readability by allowing related definitions to be scanned without interrupting the flow of the surrounding content. Publishing systems, accessibility technologies, and content management systems rely on correctly structured definition lists to preserve the relationship between each term and its description across different output formats.

In well-structured HTML, term lists are authored either as native <dl> elements containing <dt> and <dd> pairs or as unordered lists where each <li> begins with a <strong> term followed by a separator and its corresponding definition. The native <dl> structure provides the clearest semantic representation, while the bold-label pattern offers an alternative that the converter can also recognize.

The converter detects both supported HTML patterns when generating DITA output. Native <dl> elements map directly to DITA <dl>, while recognized <ul> lists that follow the bold-label pattern are converted to the same DITA definition list structure. Each term becomes a DITA <dt>, each definition becomes a <dd>, and related pairs are grouped within a <dlentry>.
conbody.note: Use native HTML <dl>, <dt>, and <dd> elements wherever possible to represent term-definition relationships. Although the converter recognizes supported <ul> patterns, native definition lists provide the clearest semantic structure and produce the most reliable conversion results.

conbody.p: Images and graphics are the primary means of communicating spatial relationships, component locations, interface states, system architectures, and process flows that text alone cannot convey efficiently. In technical publications, the image or graphic and its surrounding context carry equal structural weight.
The key differences between images and graphics are outlined below:

ul.li: An image is a raster file — a grid of pixels captured or rendered at a fixed resolution. Images are resolution dependent, when scaled up beyond their original size, they lose sharpness. For example, screenshots, photographs, and scanned content (PNG, JPEG, BMP).

A graphic is a vector-based or constructed visual — built from mathematical shapes, lines, curves, and text rather than pixels. Graphics are resolution independent, when scaled up beyond their size does not lose its quality. For example, diagrams, flowcharts, and schematic illustrations (SVG, EMF, Visio, PDF).

conbody.note: Embed every image directly in the document body, apply meaningful alt text for accessibility, and add a caption to every figure that requires a title in the published output.
conbody.p: In well-structured HTML, images are referenced through valid src paths and positioned according to their intended role within the document. Images placed between block-level elements typically represent standalone figures, while images embedded within a paragraph support the surrounding text. When a <figure> element includes a <figcaption>, the caption provides a descriptive title for the generated figure.

concept.abstract: This section covers the Table style in HTML — the primary structure for presenting information with inherent row-and-column relationships — and ten scenarios: a standard multi-column table, a table with a caption, a table with no header row, merged cells, nested tables, lists and images inside table cells, tables spanning multiple pages, consecutive tables, and a two-column parameter table in a reference topic. The converter reads each table's structure, cell complexity, and topic context to determine whether to map it to <simpletable>, a CALS <table>, or <properties>.

conbody.p: ATable is the primary structure for reference and lookup content. It is a structural mechanism to present information that has inherent row-and-column relationships — parameter names and their values, feature names and their states, error codes and their meanings, API fields and their data types.

A table reduces a lookup task from reading a paragraph to scanning a row and column. In DITA-XML, a table is structured data — each cell is a discrete, addressable unit that a transform can reformat for PDF, or online help output, filter by column for conditional publishing, and extract independently for reuse in other deliverables.

A table is an HTML structure used to organize related information into rows and columns. Represented by the native <table> element together with <tr>, <th>, and <td>, it presents information that is easier to compare, scan, or reference than the same information written as continuous text. Tables commonly represent configuration parameters, feature comparisons, error codes, API fields, and other structured lookup information.

The converter evaluates each table's structure — merged cells, the presence of a <caption>, column count, and the topic type it appears in — to determine the correct DITA output. A simple table maps to <simpletable>. A table with merged cells or a <caption> maps to a CALS <table> with <tgroup>. A two-column parameter table inside a Reference topic maps to <properties>. The converter relies entirely on the HTML table model, never on visual appearance.
conbody.note: Author tables using native <table>, <tr>, <th>, and <td> elements. Tables simulated with spacing, <pre>, or images are converted as plain text or figures, with no table structure in the output.

conbody.p: Admonitions are paragraph-level notices that separate advisory, safety-related, or supplementary information from the surrounding body content. Admonitions identify information that requires immediate reader attention — safety warnings, usage restrictions, helpful tips, important prerequisites, and cautionary notices — and give it structural separation from the prose that surrounds it.

For readers and publishing systems, admonition apply stronger visual treatment or weight from tip through note through caution through warning through danger. Each one of them are distinct in admonition icons, background color, or text color.

The converter maps a paragraph with a recognized admonition style directly to <note type="[type]">. For a bold inline label, it applies content pattern recognition: it reads the opening text, removes the label, and maps the remaining text to the matching note type.

ul.li: A cross-reference is an active, field-based link to a heading, figure, table, footnote, or bookmark within the same document or internal identifier (such as bookmark).

A bookmarkassigns a named identifier to a specific location in the document — a word, a phrase, a paragraph, or a position between characters. Bookmarks serve as anchor points that cross-references and hyperlinks can target.Both cross-reference and/or bookmarks target updates automatically when the document is restructured or the sections are moved within the same document.

A hyperlinkstores an explicit address — a URL, an email address, a file path, or a sometimes same-document bookmark anchor. Unlike bookmark and cross reference, the hyperlink address is fixed at the time of creation.Using the document's native link tools is the condition that produces a valid, resolvable element in the DITA output. A link typed as plain text produces no link structure and maps to a plain

element.

conbody.p: Topic type classification is the process of assigning a heading-delimited section of HTML content to a specific DITA topic type. Unlike DITA, HTML does not explicitly identify a section as conceptual, procedural, reference, or troubleshooting content. Instead, the structure and purpose of a section are inferred from the heading and the HTML elements that follow it until the next heading of the same or higher level.

Accurate classification matters because every DITA topic type generates a distinct body element — <conbody>, <taskbody>, <refbody>, <troublebody>, or <body> — and each body element supports a specific content structure required for that topic type. A help system that filters search results by topic type, a content management system that applies different review workflows to tasks versus references, or a PDF generator that styles procedures with numbered callouts, all depend on the topic type being assigned correctly at conversion time.
conbody.note: The HTML-to-DITA converter evaluates two complementary signals when determining the topic type. The converter first evaluates the wording of the heading. It then analyzes the dominant HTML structure beneath that heading. This structure could include paragraphs, ordered lists, tables, or other recurring content patterns. When both signals indicate the same type of content, the converter generates the corresponding DITA topic and body element. It then restructures the HTML content into the child elements required by that topic type.

conbody.p: A reference section is recognized by a noun-phrase heading containing a lookup keyword such as "Supported File Formats," "Error Codes," or "API Parameters," paired with a table or parameter list as the dominant body structure. The heading keyword is the primary classification signal. A section containing only a table but no lookup keyword in the heading may be classified as Concept or Generic depending on the surrounding context.

When these signals align, the converter generates a <reference> element with <refbody>. The opening paragraph maps to <shortdesc>. Any introductory prose appearing before the first table is wrapped in a <section> element inside <refbody> rather than placed directly in <refbody>. A 2-column table in a section whose heading contains an API keyword such as "API," "parameters," "fields," or "attributes" maps to <properties>. The same 2-column table in a reference section without an API keyword maps to <simpletable>.

conbody.p: A troubleshooting section is recognized by a problem-oriented heading such as "The Printer Does Not Power On" or "Print Jobs Fail to Complete," paired with a body that presents a condition, a cause, and a corrective action. The converter looks for bold labels in the form Cause: and Remedy: in the body. Both the heading and the body labels must be present. A problem-oriented heading without cause and remedy labels causes the converter to classify the section as Task or Generic depending on the body structure.

When these signals align, the converter generates a <troubleshooting> element with <troublebody>. The problem heading maps to <title> and the condition text maps to <condition>. Each cause label and its associated text maps to <cause> inside a <troubleSolution> block. Each remedy label and its associated steps maps to <remedy> inside the same <troubleSolution> block, with each <li> mapping to <step><cmd>. When a section contains multiple cause-and-remedy pairs, the converter generates one <condition> at the top of <troublebody> and a separate <troubleSolution> for each pair. The condition is not repeated for each solution.

concept.shortdesc: A Generic topic is the converter's fallback classification when the heading and body content together

conbody.p: A Generic topic is the converter's fallback classification when the heading and body content together do not provide sufficient signals to identify a Concept, Task, Reference, or Troubleshooting pattern. The most common triggers are a descriptive heading followed only by a <ul> list, mixed body content where no single element type is dominant, a heading verb and body structure that conflict, or a section with no introductory paragraph and no table or ordered list. A <ul> list on its own never triggers task classification — task classification requires both an imperative heading and an <ol> as the primary body content.

When Generic classification is assigned, the converter generates a standard <topic> element with <body>. All supported HTML elements are mapped in document order without applying the specialized structures associated with other topic types. When no introductory paragraph is present, the converter writes an empty <shortdesc> and flags it at WARNING severity in the conversion report. Generic topics are also flagged as candidates for manual reclassification if the content appears to match a more specific topic type.
